children.value: In Homework 1 and the lectures, we studied tight-binding models with a single site in each unit cell. In that case, after a Fourier transform, the Bloch Hamiltonian is essentially a scalar function

children.html: E(k)E(\mathbf{k})E(k)

children.value: In this homework we make the
: put more than one site in a unit cell. The Bloch Hamiltonian then becomes a matrix,

children.html: H(k)=(⋯⋯⋯⋯),H(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{pmatrix} \cdots & \cdots \\ \cdots & \cdots \end{pmatrix},H(k)=(⋯⋯​⋯⋯​),

children.value: and its eigenvectors acquire internal structure. We will see that this apparently small change allows qualitatively new phenomena:

children.html: destructive interference⟶flat bands\boxed{\text{destructive interference} \longrightarrow \text{flat bands}}destructive interference⟶flat bands​
band touching⟶Dirac physics.\boxed{\text{band touching} \longrightarrow \text{Dirac physics}.}band touching⟶Dirac physics.​

children.value: The central question of this homework is therefore:
What new physics becomes possible when a unit cell contains more than one basis site?
After completing this homework, you should be able to:
construct a Bloch Hamiltonian for a lattice with multiple sites per unit cell;
distinguish information contained in band energies from information contained in Bloch eigenvectors;
derive and interpret a simple flat band;
connect a flat band to destructive interference and compact localized states;
transfer a local interference mechanism from one lattice geometry to another;
derive the honeycomb-lattice band structure and identify its gapless points;
obtain a low-energy Dirac Hamiltonian by expanding around a band-touching point;
express a two-band Hamiltonian in the Pauli-matrix basis;
determine which perturbations shift a Dirac point and which perturbations open a gap.
